---
title: "An animation with no pixels in it"
description: "anim_save(\".svg\") writes a keyframe animation as a single animated SVG: every frame emitted as vector markup, stepped by CSS, crisp at any size, and held still for a reader who asked for no motion."
categories: [Animation]
image: figs/animated-svg-poster.png
---

```{r}
#| include: false
source("_helper.R")
```

A GIF of a chart is a stack of screenshots. Zoom in and it blurs, print it and it is
96 dpi forever, and the text in it is a picture of text. But an animation built from
keyframes does not have to be raster at all: each frame is a solved scene, and a
solved scene can be written as vector markup.

`anim_save()` picks its format from the extension, and `.svg` gives you one animated
SVG: every frame emitted in full, shown in turn by a CSS step animation. No
JavaScript, nothing to load, one file.

The data is R's `USPersonalExpenditure`: five spending categories, measured every five
years from 1940 to 1960. The same five categories appear in every year, so each bar
has a stable identity (its category, the discrete `x`) and the engine tweens it from
one year's length and colour to the next.

```{r}
x <- USPersonalExpenditure
spend <- data.frame(
  category = rep(rownames(x), ncol(x)),
  year     = rep(colnames(x), each = nrow(x)),
  billions = as.vector(x)
)

a <- vplot(spend, width = 6.5, height = 3.2) |>
  mark_bar(x = category, y = billions, fill = billions) |>
  coord_flip() |>
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#e6d3a8", high = "#7a2e0e") |>
  guides(fill = "none") |>
  labs(title = "US personal expenditure, {closest_state}",
       x = NULL, y = "billions of dollars") |>
  transition_states(year, transition_length = 2, state_length = 1) |>
  ease_aes("cubic-in-out", color = "linear") |>
  animate(fps = 25, nframes = 150)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
dir.create("figs", showWarnings = FALSE)
anim_save("figs/animated-svg.svg", a)
# A one-frame poster for the gallery card: the last year.
render_plot(
  vplot(spend[spend$year == "1960", ], width = 6.5, height = 3.2) |>
    mark_bar(x = category, y = billions, fill = billions) |>
    coord_flip() |>
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#e6d3a8", high = "#7a2e0e",
                        limits = range(spend$billions)) |>
    guides(fill = "none") |>
    labs(title = "US personal expenditure, 1960",
         x = NULL, y = "billions of dollars"),
  "figs/animated-svg-poster.png", dpi = 100
)
knitr::include_graphics("figs/animated-svg.svg")
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
anim_save("spending.svg", a)
```

Three things in that code are about the animation rather than the chart:

- `{closest_state}` in the title is a frame variable. Title, subtitle and caption text
  is evaluated on every frame, so the year changes in step with the bars, flipping
  halfway through each move.
- `ease_aes("cubic-in-out", color = "linear")` gives the bars two clocks. Position
  and length follow the cubic curve: each move starts slowly, speeds up and settles
  gently into the next year. Colour gets its own linear easing, so the fill changes
  at a constant rate across the whole move instead of bunching up in the middle. The
  other classes are `size` and `alpha` (the latter also times marks fading in and
  out); x and y share one positional curve.
- `wrap = TRUE`, the default, slides 1960 back to 1940 to close the loop.

Two more things come free with the format. It is resolution-independent, so it is as
crisp on a retina screen or at 400% zoom as it is here. And it honours
`prefers-reduced-motion`: a reader whose system says "do not animate" gets the first
frame, held. That is handled inside the SVG itself rather than by a script that may
or may not run.

## When not to use it

An animated SVG emits *every frame in full*, so its weight grows with marks times
frames, where a raster format's does not. That makes the trade sharp rather than a
matter of taste:

- Line art, a handful of moving marks, the ordinary explanatory animation: SVG wins
  outright. This one is under 1 MB of markup and about 15 KB once the web server compresses
  it.
- A dense scatter or a datashaded field: a raster format (`.gif`, or `.png` for an
  animated PNG) is the right answer.

`anim_save()` will tell you when a `.svg` scene is dense enough that GIF or APNG
would likely be smaller, so you do not have to guess. A few hundred moving marks are
still fine as SVG: see [the animated gapminder bubble chart](gapminder.qmd).

An animation also goes into a widget: `vellumwidget::as_widget()` accepts a
`vellum_animation` and embeds it with play/pause and a frame scrubber. Since every
mark moves each frame there is no per-element interaction index behind it: you can
stop it and scrub it, but the marks do not respond to hover.
